items.title: The 'Indian Renaissance' — Context & Character
items.body:
## Why the reforms arose

- 19th-century Indian society was burdened with **Sati, child marriage, female infanticide, untouchability, caste rigidity and religious orthodoxy**.
- **Western education, liberal ideas and global influences** (French/American Revolutions), together with a critique of colonial exploitation, inspired educated Indians to reform.

## Twin thrust of the movements

- **Religious reform** — attack idolatry, superstition and priestly monopoly; return to 'pure' scripture (Vedas / Quran / rationalism).
- **Social reform** — abolish evils against women and lower castes; promote education, widow remarriage and equality.

## Significance

- Often called the **'Indian Renaissance'** — a revival of rational inquiry and cultural pride.
- Fostered a **collective identity** that fed the later **nationalist movement**.
keyPoints: Reform targeted Sati, child marriage, female infanticide, untouchability and caste rigidity.
Stimuli were Western education, liberal ideas and revolutionary influences plus a colonial critique.
Movements had a religious wing (anti-idolatry, back-to-scripture) and a social wing (women/caste uplift).
The reform era is called the 'Indian Renaissance' and helped seed Indian nationalism.

items.title: Brahmo Samaj Lineage & Young Bengal
items.body:
## Brahmo Samaj and its splits

| Leader | Body | Year | Thrust |
|---|---|---|---|
| Raja Ram Mohan Roy | Brahmo Samaj | 1828 | Monotheism; abolition of Sati (1829) |
| Debendranath Tagore | Adi Brahmo Samaj | 1842 | Rational study of Indian traditions |
| Keshab Chandra Sen | Brahmo Samaj of India | 1866 | Caste abolition; universal religion |

- **Raja Ram Mohan Roy** — 'father of the Indian Renaissance'; his campaign secured **Regulation XVII of 1829** banning Sati; backed **women's education and inheritance rights**.

## Young Bengal Movement

- Led by **Henry Louis Vivian Derozio** (Hindu College, Calcutta).
- Radical **rationalism and free thought** inspired by the **French Revolution**; attacked superstition and championed women's education.
keyPoints: Ram Mohan Roy founded the Brahmo Samaj (1828); Sati was banned by Regulation XVII of 1829.
Debendranath Tagore founded the Adi Brahmo Samaj (1842).
Keshab Chandra Sen founded the Brahmo Samaj of India (1866), stressing caste abolition and universal religion.
The Young Bengal Movement under Derozio preached rationalism and free thought inspired by the French Revolution.

items.title: Arya Samaj, Prarthana Samaj & Ramakrishna Mission
items.body:
## Arya Samaj (1875) — Dayananda Saraswati

- Call to **'Go back to the Vedas'**; opposed **idol worship, caste rigidity and rituals**.
- Launched the **Shuddhi** (reconversion) movement; promoted **gender equality**. Key text: *Satyarth Prakash*.

## Prarthana Samaj (1867) — M.G. Ranade

- Western-India counterpart of the Brahmo Samaj; worked for **caste equality, widow remarriage, women's education** and **Hindu-Muslim unity**.

## Ramakrishna Mission (1897) — Swami Vivekananda

- Founded by **Vivekananda**, disciple of **Ramakrishna Paramahamsa**.
- Combined **social service and education** with **Vedanta**; Vivekananda's **1893 Chicago Parliament of Religions** address projected Indian culture globally.
keyPoints: Dayananda Saraswati founded the Arya Samaj (1875): 'back to the Vedas', Shuddhi movement, Satyarth Prakash.
M.G. Ranade co-founded the Prarthana Samaj (1867) for caste equality and widow remarriage.
Vivekananda founded the Ramakrishna Mission (1897) for social service and Vedanta.
Vivekananda addressed the World Parliament of Religions at Chicago in 1893.

items.title: Women's Reform & Community Reform (Muslim, Parsi, Sikh)
items.body:
## Women-centred reform & legislation

- **Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar** — **Hindu Widows' Remarriage Act (1856)**; opposed child marriage and polygamy.
- **Behramji Malabari** — campaign against child marriage led to the **Age of Consent Act (1891)**.
- **Savitribai Phule** — among India's first female teachers; fought female infanticide.
- **Pandita Ramabai** (Sharda Sadan) and **Annie Besant** (Women's India Association, BHU) advanced women's education.

## Muslim, Parsi and Sikh reform

| Movement | Community | Leader |
|---|---|---|
| Aligarh Movement (MAO College) | Muslims (modern education) | Sir Syed Ahmad Khan |
| Deoband School | Muslims (orthodox education) | Deoband ulema |
| Ahmadiyya (1889) | Muslims (universal brotherhood) | Mirza Ghulam Ahmad |
| Rahnumai Mazdayasnan Sabha (1851) | Parsis | Dadabhai Naoroji |
| Singh Sabha / Akali | Sikhs (Gurudwara reform) | Singh Sabha leaders |
keyPoints: Vidyasagar drove the Hindu Widows' Remarriage Act (1856); Malabari the Age of Consent Act (1891).
Savitribai Phule, Pandita Ramabai and Annie Besant advanced women's education.
Aligarh Movement (Sir Syed Ahmad Khan) promoted modern Muslim education; Deoband stressed orthodox education.
Ahmadiyya (Mirza Ghulam Ahmad, 1889), Rahnumai Mazdayasnan Sabha (Parsi, Naoroji) and Singh Sabha/Akali (Sikh) reformed their communities.

items.title: Anti-Caste & Self-Respect Movements
items.body:
## Challenging caste hierarchy

| Movement | Region | Year | Leader |
|---|---|---|---|
| Satyashodhak Samaj | Maharashtra | 1873 | Jyotirao Phule |
| Aravippuram / SNDP | Kerala | 1888 / 1903 | Sree Narayana Guru |
| Justice Party | Madras | 1916 | T.M. Nair, P. Tyagaraja Chetti |
| Self-Respect Movement | Tamil Nadu | 1925 | Periyar E.V. Ramaswami |
| Depressed Classes (Mahars) | Maharashtra | 1924 | B.R. Ambedkar |

- **Jyotirao Phule** — founded the **Satyashodhak Samaj (1873)**, opposed Brahminical dominance, wrote ***Gulamgiri***, opened schools for lower castes and girls.
- **Sree Narayana Guru** — 'One caste, one religion, one God'; **Aravippuram** consecration (1888); **SNDP** (1903) for the Ezhavas.
- **Periyar** — rationalist **Self-Respect Movement**; journal ***Kudi Arasu***.
- **Justice Party** agitation led to a **1930 Government Order** granting reservations.
keyPoints: Jyotirao Phule founded the Satyashodhak Samaj (1873) and wrote Gulamgiri against caste oppression.
Sree Narayana Guru led the Aravippuram (1888) / SNDP (1903) movement: 'One caste, one religion, one God'.
The Justice Party (Madras, 1916) opposed Brahmin dominance; its stir led to a 1930 reservation order.
Periyar's Self-Respect Movement (Tamil Nadu, 1925) was rationalist; his journal was Kudi Arasu.

items.title: Reform in Andhra — Veeresalingam, Gurajada, Naidu, Gidugu
items.body:
## Kandukuri Veeresalingam (1848–1919)

- Regarded as the **father of the Telugu Renaissance** and of modern Telugu social reform.
- Organised the **first widow remarriage in the Telugu region at Rajahmundry (1881)**; campaigned against **dowry, child marriage and the nautch (devadasi) system** and founded **schools for girls**.
- Edited the reformist journal ***Vivekavardhini***; wrote ***Rajasekhara Charitramu*** (an early Telugu social novel). His reform work drew on **Brahmo Samaj** ideals.

## Gurajada Apparao (1862–1915)

- Wrote ***Kanyasulkam*** (1892), the **first modern Telugu play**, satirising the sale of girls in marriage and child marriage.
- Pioneered **spoken (vaaduka) Telugu** in literature; wrote the patriotic poem ***Desamunu Preminchumanna*** ('Love your country').

## Raghupati Venkataratnam Naidu (1862–1939)

- A leading **Brahmo Samaj** reformer in the Andhra/Madras region; led the **anti-nautch (anti-devadasi)** and **social-purity / temperance** movements. Noted educationist (Principal, Pithapuram Rajah's College, Kakinada).

## Gidugu Venkata Ramamurthy (1863–1940)

- Champion of **Vyavaharika Bhasha (spoken Telugu)** against the classical **Grandhika** style; studied the **Savara tribal language**. His birthday, **29 August, is Telugu Language Day**.

> Note: some digests loosely list Veeresalingam under 'Veda Samaj' (a Madras body linked to Chembeti Sridharalu Naidu); his own work was centred on the Rajahmundry reform associations and Brahmo ideals.
keyPoints: Kandukuri Veeresalingam — father of the Telugu Renaissance; first Telugu-region widow remarriage (Rajahmundry, 1881); journal Vivekavardhini; novel Rajasekhara Charitramu.
Gurajada Apparao wrote Kanyasulkam (1892) against bride-price/child marriage and championed spoken Telugu; poem Desamunu Preminchumanna.
Raghupati Venkataratnam Naidu led the Brahmo Samaj in Andhra and the anti-nautch and social-purity/temperance movements.
Gidugu Venkata Ramamurthy led the Vyavaharika Bhasha (spoken-Telugu) movement and studied Savara; 29 August is Telugu Language Day.

items.title: Reform Journals, Legal Cases, Schools & Theosophy (PYQ set)
items.body:
## Dalit journalism & Keshab Chandra Sen

- **Gopal Baba Walangkar** published ***Vital-Vidhvansak*** (1888) — regarded as the **first monthly for the 'untouchables'/Depressed Classes**; an early associate of Phule/Ambedkarite thought.
- **Keshab Chandra Sen** founded the **Indian Reform Association (1870)** and the **'Church/Tabernacle of the New Dispensation' (Nava Vidhan, 1880)**; he was earlier linked to the **Calcutta Unitarian Committee**.

## Landmark women's reform cases & schools

- **Rakhmabai case (1884–88)** — a woman's refusal of restitution of conjugal rights; the controversy touched **women's education, the age of consent and restitution of conjugal rights**, and pushed the **Age of Consent Act (1891)**.
- **Bethune School (Calcutta, 1849)** — founded by **J.E.D. Bethune**; **Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar** was its secretary and a champion of female education.

## Reform-era texts & chronology

| Work | Author | Year |
|---|---|---|
| ***Neel Darpan*** (indigo planters' oppression) | Dinabandhu Mitra | **1860** |
| Arya Samaj founded | Dayananda Saraswati | **1875** |
| ***Anandamath*** (Vande Mataram) | Bankim Chandra Chatterjee | **1882** |

## Theosophical Society

- Founded by **Madame H.P. Blavatsky & Colonel H.S. Olcott** in **New York (1875)**; Indian headquarters shifted to **Adyar, Madras (1882)**. **Annie Besant** later led it, founded the Central Hindu School (→ BHU) and the Home Rule League.
keyPoints: Gopal Baba Walangkar's Vital-Vidhvansak (1888) = first monthly for the Depressed Classes/'untouchables'.
Keshab Chandra Sen: Indian Reform Association (1870) & Church of the New Dispensation (Nava Vidhan, 1880); Calcutta Unitarian Committee link.
Rakhmabai case (1884) touched women's education, age of consent & restitution of conjugal rights; fed the Age of Consent Act 1891.
Bethune School (1849, J.E.D. Bethune) — Vidyasagar its secretary; female education.
Chronology: Neel Darpan (1860) < Arya Samaj (1875) < Anandamath (1882).
Theosophical Society: Blavatsky & Olcott (New York 1875); HQ Adyar, Madras (1882); later Annie Besant.
items.mnemonic: Reform-text order: Neel Darpan 1860 → Arya Samaj 1875 → Anandamath 1882.
